To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
participants who lose weight in a behavioral weight management program perceive themselves to have become less attractive and that this perception is unrelated to their actual weight loss.

there was little relationship between objectively-measured and perceived weight changes, but a strong relationship between perceived weight and attractiveness changes, among participants in a behavioral treatment for obesity.
there is little correspondence between objectively measured weight change and perceived changes in weight or attractiveness and that perceptions of weight and attractiveness are highly related.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between objective and subjective weight changes in a weight control setting.
the relationship between objective and perceived changes in body weight and attractiveness.
the relationship between objectively measured weight change and changes in perceived body weight, and perceived attractiveness.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the participants' perceptions of changes in their attractiveness were related to the actual weight change they experienced and that the perceptions of weight and attractiveness change were related to each other.
perceived attractiveness is a more sensitive indicator of change in weight than is objective weight change.
perceived changes in attractiveness were more closely associated with changes in weight, as perceived by the participants, than were actual changes in weight.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
weight loss and attractiveness are not the same.

the participants in this weight control program perceived that they were losing weight and that they were becoming more attractive, but that their perceptions were not based on objective measures of their weight changes.
the appearance changes associated with participation are more related to changes in attractiveness than to changes in weight.
The main takeaway from our work is that
people’s perception of weight change and their perception of change in attractiveness are not necessarily related to their actual weight change.
people’s perceptions of their weight and attractiveness may not always match up with their actual weight changes.
weight loss programs need to be more focused on helping people feel more attractive, not just lose weight.
